claim: Approximately 6% of megakaryocytes in healthy C57Bl/6 murine marrow contain at least one neutrophil.
source: Whole-mount 3-dimensional (3D) immunofluorescence imaging of healthy C57Bl/6 murine marrow revealed that ~6% of MKs contain at least one neutrophil, and occasionally other bone marrow cells (Figure 1A and Video 1).
evidence: Quantitative data from immunofluorescence imaging of murine marrow, supported by Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: Emperipolesis is observable in unmanipulated human marrow.
source: Emperipolesis was similarly evident upon confocal imaging of unmanipulated human marrow (Figure 1B).
evidence: Direct observation via confocal microscopy shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Murine megakaryocytes derived from bone marrow or fetal liver are efficient at emperipolesis with approximately 20-40% of MKs participating.
source: Murine MKs, derived either from bone marrow or fetal liver cells, were efficient at emperipolesis (~20–40% of MKs).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from in vitro co-culture experiments.

claim: Neutrophils are the most common cell type participating in emperipolesis.
source: Neutrophils were by far the most common participants, although B220+ B cells, CD115+ monocytes, and occasional CD3+ T cells and NK1.1+ NK cells were also observed within MKs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of cell types shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Human cultured megakaryocytes exhibit less efficient emperipolesis (2-5% of MKs) compared to murine MKs.
source: Emperipolesis was less efficient in human cultured MKs (2–5% of MKs), which are typically smaller than murine MKs
evidence: Comparative quantitative data from human and murine MK cultures.

claim: Neutrophil transit through megakaryocytes can be completed in as little as a few minutes.
source: Live cell imaging of murine MKs co-incubated with fresh bone marrow cells showed that neutrophil transit was of variable duration, in some cases lasting only a few minutes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and Videos 2, 3 and 5)
evidence: Direct observation via live cell imaging documented in figures and videos.

claim: Neutrophils enter megakaryocytes within membrane-bound vacuoles called emperisomes.
source: Second, neutrophils enter MKs within membrane-bound vacuoles, hereafter termed emperisomes, bearing the MK surface marker CD41+ (Figure 2A and Video 3).
evidence: Confocal microscopy showing CD41+ membrane surrounding neutrophils, as shown in Figure 2A and Video 3.

claim: After neutrophil uptake into the emperisome, the vacuolar space between neutrophil and MK is resorbed such that neutrophil and MK membranes become closely apposed.
source: After neutrophil uptake into the emperisome (Figure 2B), the vacuolar space between neutrophil and MK was resorbed such that neutrophil and MK membranes became closely apposed, resulting in a structure composed of two membrane leaflets surrounding the neutrophil (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Electron microscopy observations shown in Figure 2B, C, and D.

claim: Eventually, only a single bilipid membrane separates the neutrophil cytoplasm from the MK cytoplasm.
source: Subsequently, only a single bilipid membrane came to separate the neutrophil cytoplasm from the MK cytoplasm, a finding that echoed the loss of CD41 staining observed by immunofluorescence, confirming dissolution of the emperisome and thereby translocation of the neutrophil to an intracytoplasmic location (Figure 2E).
evidence: Electron microscopy and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Emperipolesis is dramatically curtailed by inhibitors of actin polymerization, cytochalasin D and latrunculin A.
source: The microtubule polymerization inhibitor nocodazole showed a negligible effect, but emperipolesis was dramatically curtailed by inhibitors of actin polymerization, cytochalasin D and latrunculin A (Figure 3A).
evidence: Experimental data using pharmacological inhibitors shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Emperipolesis requires active cytoskeletal engagement by both megakaryocytes and neutrophils.
source: This effect was observed when either MKs or marrow cells were exposed to these inhibitors, confirming obligate active cytoskeletal engagement by both participants (Figure 3B, controls of actin inhibition in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental data showing effects of inhibitors on either cell type, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Neutrophils entering megakaryocytes exhibit a polarized appearance.
source: Consistent with these results, neutrophils entering MKs exhibited a polarized appearance, while MKs developed a transcellular cup similar to that observed in endothelial cells during transendothelial migration of leukocytes (Carman and Springer, 2004; Ley et al., 2007) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, and Video 2).
evidence: Microscopy observations shown in figures and videos, with comparison to published literature on transendothelial migration.

claim: Megakaryocytes develop a transcellular cup during emperipolesis similar to that observed in endothelial cells during transendothelial migration of leukocytes.
source: Consistent with these results, neutrophils entering MKs exhibited a polarized appearance, while MKs developed a transcellular cup similar to that observed in endothelial cells during transendothelial migration of leukocytes (Carman and Springer, 2004; Ley et al., 2007) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, and Video 2).
evidence: Microscopy observations with comparison to published literature on transendothelial migration (Carman and Springer, 2004; Ley et al., 2007).

claim: Actin localizes to the interface between megakaryocytes and extracellular neutrophils and encases neutrophil-containing CD41+ vacuoles.
source: In agreement with inhibitor findings, actin but not microtubules localized to the interface between MKs and extracellular neutrophils and was observed to encase neutrophil-containing CD41+ vacuoles (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Actin is not observed surrounding neutrophils that are no longer delimited by CD41-expressing membrane.
source: by contrast, actin was not observed surrounding neutrophils that were no longer delimited by CD41-expressing membrane (Figure 3C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Blockade of β2 integrin CD18 strongly impairs emperipolesis.
source: However, blockade of the β2 integrin CD18, expressed by neutrophils but not MKs, strongly impaired emperipolesis (Figure 3D).
evidence: Experimental data using blocking antibodies shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CD18-deficient bone marrow cells exhibit reduced emperipolesis into wild-type megakaryocytes.
source: Correspondingly, CD18-deficient bone marrow cells exhibited reduced emperipolesis into WT MKs (Figure 3E)
evidence: Experimental data using CD18-deficient cells shown in Figure 3E.

claim: ICAM-1 is expressed by a population of human and murine megakaryocytes.
source: Confocal microscopy showed that ICAM-1 is expressed by a population of human and murine MKs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: Confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: Emperipolesis by ICAM-1-deficient megakaryocytes is significantly impaired.
source: In agreement with previous observations in rat (Tanaka et al., 1997), emperipolesis by ICAM-1-deficient MKs was significantly impaired (Figure 3F).
evidence: Experimental data using ICAM-1-deficient MKs shown in Figure 3F, with reference to prior rat studies (Tanaka et al., 1997).

claim: Inhibition of ezrin phosphorylation impairs emperipolesis.
source: Inhibition of ezrin phosphorylation impaired emperipolesis (Figure 3G, controls of ezrin inhibition in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Experimental data using ezrin inhibitor shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Ezrin co-localizes strongly with ICAM-1 at sites of megakaryocyte contact with tethered neutrophils.
source: By confocal microscopy, ezrin could be detected only at sites of MK contact with tethered neutrophils, where it co-localized strongly with ICAM-1, consistent with its role as a bridge to the cytoskeleton (Figure 3H and I).
evidence: Confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3H and I.

claim: Ezrin cannot be visualized in megakaryocytes not tethered to leukocytes or with only internalized leukocytes.
source: By contrast, ezrin could not be visualized in MKs not tethered to leukocytes, or with only internalized leukocytes (Figure 3H).
evidence: Confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Emperipolesis is mediated in part by an interaction between neutrophil β2 integrins and megakaryocyte ICAM-1/ezrin during neutrophil entry.
source: Together, these data show that emperipolesis is mediated in part by an interaction between neutrophil β2 integrins and MK ICAM-1/ezrin during neutrophil entry.
evidence: Synthesis of experimental findings from blocking studies, knockout cells, and co-localization data.

claim: Absence or blockade of β2 integrins, ICAM-1, or ezrin results in only partial impairment of emperipolesis, indicating a role for alternate mechanisms.
source: However, absence or blockade of these factors resulted in only partial impairment of emperipolesis, indicating a role for alternate mechanisms not yet defined.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing incomplete inhibition of emperipolesis.

claim: Neutrophils engaged in emperipolesis frequently localize to the demarcation membrane system (DMS).
source: As observed by others (Centurione et al., 2004; Thiele et al., 1984), neutrophils engaged in emperipolesis frequently localized to the DMS, the intracytoplasmic membrane network implicated in platelet production (Figure 4A).
evidence: Electron microscopy observations shown in Figure 4A, with reference to prior studies (Centurione et al., 2004; Thiele et al., 1984).

claim: Membrane contiguity exists between intracytoplasmic neutrophils and the demarcation membrane system.
source: Close examination of this interaction demonstrated membrane contiguity between the neutrophil and the DMS, suggesting that neutrophils might be able to serve as membrane donors to MKs and potentially to platelets (Figure 4A).
evidence: Electron microscopy observations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Neutrophils inside but not outside megakaryocytes show substantial loss of CellVue maroon membrane staining.
source: Confocal microscopy showed substantial loss of CellVue maroon staining in neutrophils inside but not outside MKs (Figure 4B).
evidence: Confocal microscopy data using membrane labeling shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Loss of fluorescence from neutrophils inside megakaryocytes is observed with multiple lipid stains (Bodipy, PKH67, CellVue maroon), excluding a non-specific chemical interaction.
source: Similar loss of fluorescence was observed with the lipid stains Bodipy and PKH67, excluding a non-specific chemical interaction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Experimental data using multiple independent lipid stains shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Time-lapse spinning disk confocal microscopy confirms transfer of neutrophil membrane to megakaryocytes from an intracellular location.
source: Finally, time-lapse spinning disk confocal microscopy confirmed transfer of neutrophil membrane to MKs from this intracellular location (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and Videos 5 and 6).
evidence: Live cell imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and Videos 5 and 6.

claim: Membrane transfer during emperipolesis is not associated with phosphatidylserine externalization onto the neutrophil surface.
source: Of note, membrane transfer during emperipolesis was not associated with phosphatidylserine externalization onto the neutrophil surface (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: Experimental data using lactadherin and Annexin V staining shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–F.

claim: Megakaryocyte-derived lipids strongly co-localize with neutrophil membrane during emperipolesis.
source: MK-derived lipids strongly co-localized with neutrophil membrane during emperipolesis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I)
evidence: Confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: Lipid exchange from neutrophils to megakaryocytes is strongly inhibited by latrunculin A.
source: While lipid exchange from neutrophils to MKs was strongly inhibited by latrunculin A, transfer from MKs to neutrophils was not (Figure 4C)
evidence: Experimental data using latrunculin A shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Transfer of membrane from megakaryocytes to neutrophils is not primarily mediated by emperipolesis.
source: While lipid exchange from neutrophils to MKs was strongly inhibited by latrunculin A, transfer from MKs to neutrophils was not (Figure 4C), suggesting that this reciprocal transfer was not mediated primarily by emperipolesis.
evidence: Inference from differential effects of latrunculin A on bidirectional membrane transfer.

claim: PKH67-stained megakaryocytes release many PKH67+ microparticles that can transfer membrane fluorescence to neutrophils in the absence of intact megakaryocytes.
source: MKs produce microparticles in great abundance (Cunin et al., 2017; Flaumenhaft et al., 2009), and PKH67-stained MKs were observed to release many PKH67 +microparticles in a latrunculin A-independent manner that could transfer membrane fluorescence to neutrophils in the absence of intact MKs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1J, with reference to prior studies (Cunin et al., 2017; Flaumenhaft et al., 2009).

claim: No fluorescence is detected on megakaryocytes cultured with supernatant from PKH67-stained marrow cells.
source: By contrast, no fluorescence was detected on MKs cultured with supernatant from PKH67-stained marrow cells, rendering unlikely a role of marrow cell-derived microparticles, exosomes or apoptotic bodies in membrane transfer from neutrophils to MKs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Neutrophils transfer plasma membrane to megakaryocytes via emperipolesis.
source: Thus, neutrophils transfer plasma membrane to MKs via emperipolesis, while reciprocal membrane exchange from MKs to neutrophils likely occurs primarily via MK microparticles, a phenomenon of interest not explored further here.
evidence: Synthesis of experimental findings on bidirectional membrane transfer.

claim: Surface biotin can be detected on some megakaryocytes after incubation with biotinylated marrow cells.
source: However, surface biotin could be detected on some MKs after incubation with biotinylated marrow cells (Figure 4D), confirming that membrane exchange from neutrophils to MK transfers proteins.
evidence: Experimental data using surface biotinylation shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Membrane exchange from neutrophils to megakaryocytes transfers proteins.
source: However, surface biotin could be detected on some MKs after incubation with biotinylated marrow cells (Figure 4D), confirming that membrane exchange from neutrophils to MK transfers proteins.
evidence: Experimental data using surface biotinylation shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Most platelets produced by donor megakaryocytes co-cultured with CellVue Maroon-stained marrow cells are positive for CellVue Maroon.
source: Remarkably, most platelets produced by donor MKs (i.e. CMFDA+) were also positive for CellVue Maroon, indicating a high frequency of incorporation of donor leukocyte membrane (Figure 5A).
evidence: In vivo platelet production assay with flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The intensity of CellVue Maroon staining on platelets produced by donor megakaryocytes remains constant over time.
source: The intensity of CellVue Maroon staining remained constant over time, suggesting that donor membrane was employed continuously over an extended period (Figure 5B).
evidence: Time-course flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Membrane fluorescence from mT/mG marrow cells efficiently transfers into wild-type megakaryocytes in vitro.
source: Confocal imaging confirmed that membrane fluorescence from mT/mG marrow cells efficiently transferred into MKs in vitro (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Membrane fluorescence is detected on platelets produced in vivo by wild-type megakaryocytes incubated with mT/mG marrow donors.
source: Membrane fluorescence was also detected on platelets produced in vivo by WT MKs incubated with mT/mG marrow donors, albeit with weaker signal since membrane fluorescence is less intense that with lipid stains (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: In vivo platelet production assay with flow cytometry shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Platelets emerging in vivo from megakaryocytes co-cultured with CellTrace Violet-stained marrow cells contain CellTrace violet.
source: Interestingly, platelets emerging in vivo contained CellTrace violet, consistent with cytoplasmic protein transfer (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: In vivo platelet production assay with flow cytometry shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Lipids and intracellular proteins are transferred from marrow cells to megakaryocytes and to their daughter platelets.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that lipids and intracellular proteins are transferred from marrow cells not only to MKs but also to their daughter platelets.
evidence: Synthesis of experimental findings from multiple labeling experiments.

claim: Biotin cannot be detected on emerging platelets when megakaryocytes were previously co-cultured with surface-biotinylated marrow cells.
source: Of note, we could not detect biotin on emerging platelet when MKs were previously co-cultured with surface-biotinylated marrow cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Experimental data using surface biotinylation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Platelets with intermediate fluorescent phenotype resulting from mT/mG→WT membrane transfer are observed in mice chimeric for WT and mT/mG marrow.
source: To this end, we generated mice chimeric for WT and mT/mG marrow, allowing us to seek platelets resulting from mT/mG→WT membrane transfer in a fully native environment. Indeed, platelets with the expected intermediate fluorescent phenotype were observed (Figure 5E)
evidence: In vivo chimeric mouse model with flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Intracellular neutrophils transfer membrane to megakaryocytes and thereby to platelets via emperipolesis in vivo.
source: We conclude that intracellular neutrophils transfer membrane to MKs and thereby to platelets via emperipolesis in vivo.
evidence: Synthesis of findings from chimeric mouse experiments and microscopy observations.

claim: An important fraction of 'red-intermediate' platelets in mT/mG/WT chimeric mice express phosphatidylserine.
source: Of note, we observed an important fraction of the 'red-intermediate' platelets in the mT/mG/WT chimeric mice expressing phosphatidylserine (Figure 5F and G; control for Annexin V staining in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: Flow cytometry data from chimeric mice shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: Red-intermediate platelets in chimeric mice show normal levels of CD62P and a marginal band of β1-tubulin by microscopy.
source: while we observe normal levels of CD62P and a marginal band of β1-tubulin by microscopy (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H–I), excluding an abnormal activation phenotype (Moskalensky et al., 2018; Sadoul, 2015).
evidence: Microscopy and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H–I, with reference to literature on platelet activation (Moskalensky et al., 2018; Sadoul, 2015).

claim: Emperipolesis-derived platelets could be functionally distinct, potentially including enhanced thrombogenic capacity.
source: This result suggests the possibility that emperipolesis-derived platelets could be functionally distinct, potentially including enhanced thrombogenic capacity.
evidence: Speculation based on observed phosphatidylserine expression and its known role in coagulation.

claim: The proportion of megakaryocytes containing at least one neutrophil increases from approximately 2-5% in control mice to approximately 6-10% under stress conditions (LPS injection and IgG-mediated thrombocytopenia).
source: The proportion of MKs containing at least one neutrophil was assessed in two-dimensional marrow sections. In each case, emperipolesis increased from a baseline of ~2–5% in control mice to ~6–10% under stress (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Quantitative histological analysis shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: Enhanced drive for platelet production following thrombopoietin administration or platelet depletion by anti-CD41 is not sufficient to augment emperipolesis.
source: Interestingly, an enhanced drive for platelet production was not sufficient to augment emperipolesis, because accelerated platelet production following administration of thrombopoietin, or platelet depletion by anti-CD41 was unaccompanied by an increase in emperipolesis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Experimental data from TPO and anti-CD41 treatments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Co-culture with living marrow cells markedly enhances pro-platelet production by megakaryocytes.
source: Co-culture with living marrow cells markedly enhanced pro-platelet production (Figure 6D).
evidence: IncuCyte live-cell microscopy data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Megakaryocytes cultured with fixed cells or cell supernatants produce fewer pro-platelets than those cultured alone.
source: By contrast, MKs cultured with fixed cells or cell supernatants produced fewer pro-platelets than those cultured alone, weighing against a role for contact and soluble factors and implicating emperipolesis directly (Figure 6D).
evidence: IncuCyte live-cell microscopy data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Megakaryocytes cultured with marrow cells are more efficient at producing platelets in vivo compared to those cultured alone.
source: As predicted by the IncuCyte findings, MKs cultured with marrow cells were more efficient at producing platelets (Figure 6E and F), consistent with promotion of thrombocytogenesis by emperipolesis.
evidence: In vivo adoptive transfer experiment with serial platelet quantitation shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Emperipolesis is a dynamic process mediated actively by both megakaryocytes and neutrophils.
source: We show here that emperipolesis is a dynamic process mediated actively by both lineages, in part through the β2-integrin/ICAM-1/ezrin pathway.
evidence: Synthesis of experimental findings on cytoskeletal requirements and molecular pathways.

claim: Tethered neutrophils enter megakaryocytes in membrane-bound vesicles before penetrating into the megakaryocyte cytoplasm.
source: Tethered neutrophils enter in membrane-bound vesicles before penetrating into the megakaryocyte cytoplasm.
evidence: Synthesis of confocal and electron microscopy observations.

claim: Intracytoplasmic neutrophils develop membrane contiguity with the demarcation membrane system, thereby transferring membrane to the megakaryocyte and to daughter platelets.
source: Intracytoplasmic neutrophils develop membrane contiguity with the demarcation membrane system, thereby transferring membrane to the megakaryocyte and to daughter platelets.
evidence: Synthesis of electron microscopy and membrane labeling experiments.

claim: Emperipolesis occurs in otherwise unmanipulated murine marrow in vivo, resulting in circulating platelets that bear membrane from non-megakaryocytic hematopoietic donors.
source: This phenomenon occurs in otherwise unmanipulated murine marrow in vivo, resulting in circulating platelets that bear membrane from non-megakaryocytic hematopoietic donors.
evidence: Findings from chimeric mouse experiments showing membrane transfer in native environment.

claim: Neutrophils egress intact from megakaryocytes after emperipolesis.
source: Transit through megakaryocytes can be completed as rapidly as minutes, after which neutrophils egress intact.
evidence: Live cell imaging showing viable neutrophils exiting MKs.

claim: Emperipolesis is amplified in models of murine inflammation associated with platelet overproduction.
source: Emperipolesis is amplified in models of murine inflammation associated with platelet overproduction, contributing to platelet production in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: Experimental data from LPS and IgG-mediated thrombocytopenia models.

claim: Emperipolesis contributes to platelet production in vitro and in vivo.
source: Emperipolesis is amplified in models of murine inflammation associated with platelet overproduction, contributing to platelet production in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: Experimental data from IncuCyte and adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: Megakaryocytes represent less than 0.3% of hematopoietic cells in bone marrow.
source: Representing less than 0.3% of hematopoietic cells in bone marrow (Levine et al., 1982; Machlus and Italiano, 2013; Winter et al., 2010), MKs interact with other hematopoietic lineages.
evidence: Reference to published literature (Levine et al., 1982; Machlus and Italiano, 2013; Winter et al., 2010).

claim: Megakaryocytes provide a niche for plasma cells.
source: MKs provide a niche for plasma cells (Winter et al., 2010)
evidence: Reference to published literature (Winter et al., 2010).

claim: Megakaryocytes promote neutrophil egress via production of CXCR2 ligand.
source: promote neutrophil egress via production of CXCR2 ligand (Köhler et al., 2011)
evidence: Reference to published literature (Köhler et al., 2011).

claim: Megakaryocytes regulate hematopoietic stem cell homeostasis.
source: and regulate hematopoietic stem cell homeostasis (Bruns et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: Reference to published literature (Bruns et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2014).

claim: Emperipolesis is observed in healthy marrow and increases with hematopoietic stress.
source: Emperipolesis is observed in healthy marrow and increases with hematopoietic stress, including in myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative disorders (Cashell and Buss, 1992; Mangi and Mufti, 1992), myelofibrosis (Centurione et al., 2004; Schmitt et al., 2002; Spangrude et al., 2016), gray platelet syndrome (Di Buduo et al., 2016; Larocca et al., 2015; Monteferrario et al., 2014), essential thrombocythemia (Cashell and Buss, 1992), and blood loss or hemorrhagic shock (Dziecioł et al., 1995; Sahebekhitiari and Tavassoli, 1976; Tavassoli, 1986).
evidence: Reference to multiple published studies documenting emperipolesis in various conditions.

claim: The preservation of emperipolesis in monkeys, mice, rats, cats and dogs implies evolutionary conservation.
source: Whereas the preservation of emperipolesis in monkeys (Stahl et al., 1991), mice (Centurione et al., 2004), rats (Tanaka et al., 1996), and cats and dogs (Scott and Friedrichs, 2009) implies evolutionary conservation
evidence: Reference to published observations across multiple species (Stahl et al., 1991; Centurione et al., 2004; Tanaka et al., 1996; Scott and Friedrichs, 2009).

claim: Emperipolesis is distinct from phagocytosis since the neutrophil actively penetrates into the megakaryocyte and survives to exit intact.
source: This process is distinct from phagocytosis since the neutrophil actively penetrates into the MK and survives to exit intact.
evidence: Inference from observations of active neutrophil participation and viable exit.

claim: Emperipolesis represents a new cell-in-cell interaction that enables neutrophils and potentially other cells passing through the megakaryocyte cytoplasm to modulate the production and membrane content of platelets.
source: These findings identify emperipolesis as a new cell-in-cell interaction that enables neutrophils and potentially other cells passing through the megakaryocyte cytoplasm to modulate the production and membrane content of platelets.
evidence: Synthesis of all experimental findings.

claim: β2 integrins and megakaryocyte ICAM-1/ezrin mediate another form of transcellular passage, the migration of neutrophils through the cell bodies of endothelial cells.
source: We identified β2 integrins and MK ICAM-1/ezrin as contributors to emperipolesis. These proteins also mediate another form of transcellular passage, the migration of neutrophils through the cell bodies of endothelial cells (Ley et al., 2007).
evidence: Reference to published literature on transendothelial migration (Ley et al., 2007).

claim: Endothelial transcellular migration is not known to involve penetration into the host cytoplasm.
source: Unlike emperipolesis, endothelial transcellular migration is not known to involve penetration into the host cytoplasm.
evidence: Comparison to established knowledge about transendothelial migration.

claim: Enhanced emperipolesis in chronic myeloproliferative disorders positively correlates with the peripheral platelet count.
source: Further, enhanced emperipolesis in chronic myeloproliferative disorders positively correlates with the peripheral platelet count (Thiele et al., 1984).
evidence: Reference to published literature (Thiele et al., 1984).

claim: Surface phosphatidylserine creates a scaffold for clotting factors and is a hallmark of pro-coagulant platelets.
source: Surface phosphatidylserine creates a scaffold for clotting factors and is a hallmark of pro-coagulant platelets (Heemskerk et al., 2013; Nagata et al., 2016).
evidence: Reference to published literature on platelet biology (Heemskerk et al., 2013; Nagata et al., 2016).

claim: Megakaryocyte microparticles are potent pro-inflammatory vectors implicated in the delivery of IL-1 during systemic inflammatory disease.
source: Our prior work had identified MK microparticles as potent pro-inflammatory vectors implicated in the delivery of IL-1 during systemic inflammatory disease (Cunin et al., 2017).
evidence: Reference to authors' prior published work (Cunin et al., 2017).

claim: Emperipolesis is a mechanism through which megakaryocytes may be able to 'groom' neutrophils and other immune lineages.
source: Further, by establishing transfer of membrane not only from donor cell to MK but also reciprocally, followed by release of viable cells back into the intercellular milieu, these studies identify emperipolesis as a mechanism through which MKs may be able to 'groom' neutrophils and other immune lineages.
evidence: Inference from observations of bidirectional membrane transfer and viable cell exit.

claim: Blocking antibodies targeting P-selectin, glycoprotein VI (GPVI), PECAM-1, CD44, and CXCR2 had no effect on emperipolesis.
source: Blocking antibodies targeting P-selectin, glycoprotein VI (GPVI), PECAM-1, CD44, and CXCR2 had no effect (not shown).
evidence: Experimental data from blocking antibody studies.

claim: Megakaryocytes do not express CD18.
source: However, blockade of the β2 integrin CD18, expressed by neutrophils but not MKs, strongly impaired emperipolesis (Figure 3D).
evidence: Implicit from statement that CD18 is expressed by neutrophils but not MKs.

claim: CD18-deficient marrows have a heightened proportion and density of neutrophils.
source: Correspondingly, CD18-deficient bone marrow cells exhibited reduced emperipolesis into WT MKs (Figure 3E), despite the heightened proportion and density of neutrophils in these marrows (Horwitz et al., 2001).
evidence: Reference to published literature (Horwitz et al., 2001).

claim: Ezrin mediates the attachment of the intracellular tail of ICAM-1 to the actin cytoskeleton.
source: In further support of this mechanism, we evaluated the role of ezrin, which mediates the attachment of the intracellular tail of ICAM-1 to the actin cytoskeleton (Heiska et al., 1998; Ley et al., 2007).
evidence: Reference to published literature (Heiska et al., 1998; Ley et al., 2007).

claim: Some megakaryocytes resemble 'reservoirs' containing dozens of neutrophils in stages 2 and 3 of emperipolesis.
source: While most MKs engaged in emperipolesis contained only one or two neutrophils, some resembled 'reservoirs' containing dozens of neutrophils in stages 2 and 3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), an appearance recognized in human marrow as well (Cashell and Buss, 1992; Larsen, 1970; Monteferrario et al., 2014; Thiele et al., 1984) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Microscopy observations with reference to published literature (Cashell and Buss, 1992; Larsen, 1970; Monteferrario et al., 2014; Thiele et al., 1984).

claim: Neutrophil transit through megakaryocytes can last more than one hour.
source: Live cell imaging of murine MKs co-incubated with fresh bone marrow cells showed that neutrophil transit was of variable duration, in some cases lasting only a few minutes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and Videos 2, 3 and 5) and in others more than one hour (Video 6).
evidence: Live cell imaging data shown in Video 6.

claim: Megakaryocytes were observed to contain B220+ B cells, CD115+ monocytes, CD3+ T cells and NK1.1+ NK cells in addition to neutrophils.
source: Neutrophils were by far the most common participants, although B220+ B cells, CD115+ monocytes, and occasional CD3+ T cells and NK1.1+ NK cells were also observed within MKs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Emperipolesis was observed in megakaryocytes cultured from marrow CD34+ cells but not from cord blood CD34+ cells.
source: and was observed in MKs cultured from marrow CD34+ cells but not from the even smaller MKs derived from cord blood CD34+ cells (Figure 1D and not shown).
evidence: Experimental observations from human MK cultures.

claim: Megakaryocytes develop a complex network of intracytoplasmic membrane termed the demarcation membrane system (DMS) that provides a membrane reservoir to enable platelet generation.
source: Mature MKs develop a complex network of intracytoplasmic membrane, termed the demarcation membrane system (DMS), that provides a membrane reservoir to enable platelet generation (Schulze et al., 2006).
evidence: Reference to published literature (Schulze et al., 2006).

claim: Megakaryocytes protrude pseudopodial extensions of membrane via the marrow sinusoids into the bloodstream, where shear stress releases fragments that become mature platelets.
source: MKs then protrude pseudopodial extensions of this membrane via the marrow sinusoids into the bloodstream, where shear stress releases fragments that become the mature platelets required for hemostasis (Junt et al., 2007).
evidence: Reference to published literature (Junt et al., 2007).

claim: Developing megakaryocytes undergo multiple rounds of endomitosis to become highly-polyploid cells averaging 20 to 100 μm in size.
source: Derived from hematopoietic stem cells, developing MKs undergo multiple rounds of endomitosis to become highly-polyploid cells averaging 20 to 100 μm in size (Levine et al., 1982; Machlus and Italiano, 2013).
evidence: Reference to published literature (Levine et al., 1982; Machlus and Italiano, 2013).

claim: Emperipolesis has been speculated to represent a sanctuary for neutrophils in an unfavorable marrow environment or a route for neutrophils to exit the bone marrow.
source: It has been speculated that MKs could represent a sanctuary for neutrophils in an unfavorable marrow environment, or a route for neutrophils to exit the bone marrow, but more typically emperipolesis is regarded as a curiosity without physiological significance (Lee, 1989; Sahebekhitiari and Tavassoli, 1976; Tavassoli, 1986).
evidence: Reference to published speculations (Lee, 1989; Sahebekhitiari and Tavassoli, 1976; Tavassoli, 1986).

claim: Emperipolesis is typically regarded as a curiosity without physiological significance.
source: It has been speculated that MKs could represent a sanctuary for neutrophils in an unfavorable marrow environment, or a route for neutrophils to exit the bone marrow, but more typically emperipolesis is regarded as a curiosity without physiological significance (Lee, 1989; Sahebekhitiari and Tavassoli, 1976; Tavassoli, 1986).
evidence: Reference to published literature (Lee, 1989; Sahebekhitiari and Tavassoli, 1976; Tavassoli, 1986).

claim: Megakaryocytes have a direct role in systemic inflammation.
source: Recently, we identified evidence for a direct role for MKs in systemic inflammation, highlighting the potential importance of the interaction of MKs with immune lineages (Cunin and Nigrovic, 2019; Cunin et al., 2017).
evidence: Reference to authors' prior published work (Cunin and Nigrovic, 2019; Cunin et al., 2017).

claim: Emperipolesis is strikingly heterogeneous in terms of megakaryocyte size, number of neutrophils, and duration.
source: Emperipolesis is nevertheless strikingly heterogeneous. For example, emperipolesis can be observed in MKs of all sizes and can last just minutes to over an hour. MKs may enclose a single neutrophil or encompass as many as 50 neutrophils (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Synthesis of observations from multiple experiments.

claim: There may be different types of emperipolesis, involving different molecular pathways and serving distinct functions.
source: These observations strongly suggest that there may be different types of emperipolesis, involving different molecular pathways and serving distinct functions that remain to be defined.
evidence: Inference from observed heterogeneity in emperipolesis.

claim: Emperipolesis is a tightly-regulated process mediated actively by both megakaryocytes and neutrophils via pathways reminiscent of leukocyte transendothelial migration.
source: We show here that emperipolesis is a tightly-regulated process mediated actively by both MKs and neutrophils via pathways reminiscent of leukocyte transendothelial migration.
evidence: Synthesis of experimental findings on molecular mechanisms.

claim: Neutrophils enter megakaryocytes within membrane-bound vesicles but then penetrate into the cell cytoplasm where they develop membrane continuity with the demarcation membrane system to transfer membrane to megakaryocytes and thereby to platelets.
source: Neutrophils enter MKs within membrane-bound vesicles but then penetrate into the cell cytoplasm, where they develop membrane continuity with the demarcation membrane system (DMS) to transfer membrane to MKs and thereby to platelets, accelerating platelet production.
evidence: Synthesis of microscopy and membrane labeling experiments.

claim: Neutrophils emerge intact from megakaryocytes carrying megakaryocyte components with them.
source: Neutrophils then emerge intact, carrying MK components with them.
evidence: Inference from live cell imaging and membrane labeling experiments.

claim: Emperipolesis mediates a novel form of material transfer between immune and hematopoietic lineages.
source: Together, these data identify emperipolesis as a previously unrecognized type of cell-in-cell interaction that mediates a novel form of material transfer between immune and hematopoietic lineages.
evidence: Synthesis of all experimental findings.
